AI Compute Stack · Part 9 · Memory

The Memory Wall: Why HBM Decides Who Wins AI

For twenty years chips learned to calculate far faster than memory could feed them. Large language models turned that gap into the defining constraint of AI: a GPU generating text spends most of its time waiting for data. This guide explains the memory wall, the stacked memory called HBM that holds it back, the three companies that make it, why it made your next laptop more expensive, and the hardware and software tricks for getting over it.

The AI boom made your laptop more expensive

In 2026 a 32 GB kit of desktop memory that cost around $110 to $140 a year earlier was selling for about $400 in one price tracker. Gartner expects combined DRAM and SSD prices to rise about 130% by the end of 2026, pushing average PC prices up 17% and PC shipments down about 10%. Counterpoint estimates the cost of materials for a smartphone could rise 15% or more. Dell raised PC prices in January.

The cause is not phones or PCs. Memory makers moved factory capacity to a specialised, far more profitable product: high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the stacked DRAM that sits beside every AI accelerator. HBM is reported sold out for 2026, and Bernstein does not expect the shortage to ease before 2027. To understand why AI needs so much of it, you need one idea: the memory wall.

What the memory wall is

The term dates to the 1990s, but the clearest recent evidence comes from Amir Gholami and colleagues' paper "AI and Memory Wall" (2024, later in IEEE Micro). Looking at twenty years of server hardware, they found peak compute grew about 3.0× every two years, while DRAM bandwidth grew about 1.6× and interconnect bandwidth about 1.4×. Compound those rates and the gap becomes enormous.

Twenty years of diverging growth

Index, year 0 = 1, log scale. Curves are the paper's average rates compounded, not measured data points. Drag the slider to see the gap after N years.

Put simply: each new chip generation can do far more maths per second, but the pipe that brings it numbers to work on widens much more slowly. If the work needs a lot of data per calculation, the chip idles.

Why large language models hit the wall so hard

Text generation has two phases. Prefill reads your whole prompt at once: lots of maths per byte, so chips stay busy. Decode then produces the answer one token at a time, and for every single token the model must read all of its weights from memory. For one user, that is roughly one calculation for every byte read.

An H100 can do about 989 trillion 16-bit operations a second but read only about 3.35 trillion bytes a second, so it needs about 295 operations per byte to stay busy (Baseten's figure). Decode for a single user offers about one. The chip spends over 99% of its potential waiting. That is why serving systems batch many users together: the same weights read once serve many requests. And it is why, at large batches, the KV cache (each conversation's stored attention state, which grows with context length) becomes the next thing clogging the memory pipe.

💡 A rule of thumb For a single user, the fastest a model can generate is roughly memory bandwidth ÷ model size in bytes. A 70-billion-parameter model in 16-bit precision is about 140 GB; on an H100 at 3.35 TB/s that caps decode at about 24 tokens per second, before any other overhead. Faster chips barely help this number. More bandwidth, or fewer bytes, does.

The roofline: when does a GPU stop waiting?

The roofline model draws this as two ceilings. Below a certain number of operations per byte, performance rises in a straight line with memory bandwidth (the sloped roof). Above it, the chip hits its compute limit (the flat roof). Drag the batch size to move a decode workload along the line.

H100 roofline for decode

Uses H100 figures (989 TFLOPS dense BF16, 3.35 TB/s). Simplification: with 16-bit weights, decode intensity ≈ batch size in operations per byte, ignoring KV-cache reads, which lower it in practice.

Speed-limit calculator

Pick a model size, a precision and a chip to see the single-user decode ceiling from the rule of thumb above.

Maximum tokens per second for one user

An upper bound: bandwidth ÷ weight bytes. Real systems are slower (KV cache, kernels, multi-GPU communication) and serve many users at once. If the model is bigger than one chip's memory, it must be split across several chips.

Inside HBM

Ordinary DRAM sits on sticks a few centimetres from the processor, connected by 64 wires per channel. HBM takes a radically different approach: stack DRAM dies vertically, drill thousands of vertical connections through them, and place the stack millimetres from the GPU on a shared silicon base. The result is a very wide, very short connection. Click the parts.

Cross-section of an HBM stack beside a GPU

Schematic, not to scale.

HBM3E vs HBM4

From design guides citing the JEDEC standards (HBM3E: JESD238; HBM4: JESD270-4, April 2025). Per-stack figures; products vary.

HBM3EHBM4
Interface width1,024 bits2,048 bits
Bandwidth per stack~1.2–1.33 TB/s~2.0 TB/s, up to ~3.3 TB/s in faster versions
Pin speedLower (the wider HBM4 bus does most of the work)6.4–12.8 Gb/s (Samsung demonstrated ~13)
Max capacity36 GB (12-high)64 GB (16-high, 32 Gb dies)
Compatibility—Not backward-compatible with HBM3/3E controllers
Base dieMade by the memory makerIncreasingly logic-process dies from TSMC or Samsung Foundry; "custom HBM" from HBM4E

The chip race is a memory race

Look at what changed between AI chip generations and memory is the headline every time. Nvidia reportedly pushed HBM4 speeds above earlier targets for Rubin, delaying suppliers' production, partly to stay ahead of AMD's MI455X.

Memory per accelerator

Vendor figures as reported. Toggle between capacity and bandwidth.

AMD's 72-GPU Helios rack adds up to more than 31 TB of HBM4 and about 1.7 PB/s of memory bandwidth. Google's Ironwood TPU carries 192 GB across eight HBM3E stacks, with 2.7 times the bandwidth of its predecessor, TPU v5p.

Three companies hold the key

Only SK hynix, Samsung and Micron make HBM at scale. SK hynix, which co-created the standard with AMD, has led since the AI boom began, but estimates of the split differ.

HBM market share by source

Each tab is a different tracker or period; they do not agree, so read them as a range.

  • Vera Rubin supply: Jensen Huang said on 5 June 2026 that all three makers had qualified for Rubin's HBM4. Nvidia has not disclosed allocations; analysts estimate SK hynix at 60–70%, Samsung 25–30% and Micron the rest. Samsung began HBM4 mass production in February 2026.
  • SK hynix goes to Wall Street: in July 2026 it listed American depositary shares at $149 each, raising about $26.5 billion, one of the largest equity offerings ever, with proceeds earmarked for HBM capacity and new fabs.
  • Next: custom HBM. HBM4E is expected in 2027 and HBM5 around 2029. Customers will be able to order base dies with their own logic (memory controllers, interfaces), made on TSMC or Samsung logic processes, which ties memory makers more tightly to individual chip designers.

Memory is now the expensive part

Epoch AI's analysis of AI chip component costs finds memory's share rising from 52% to 63%, while packaging and other parts shrank. Total component spending on AI chips grew from about $22 billion in 2024 to $52 billion in 2025, with HBM alone accounting for roughly $20 billion of that increase.

Memory's share of AI chip component costs

Source: Epoch AI, AI chip component cost shares. Secondary estimates put HBM3E at about $300 per stack and HBM4 at about $500 (unverified).

The consumer bill

Every wafer turned into HBM is a wafer not turned into ordinary DRAM, and an HBM stack uses several times the silicon of the same capacity of standard memory. As makers reallocated, consumer supply tightened.

What the memory crunch did to prices

Forecasts and reports from different sources and dates; not directly comparable.

Sources: Gartner, IDC, Counterpoint (via Bloomberg and trade press). Bloomberg reports some memory prices more than 10 times their January 2025 levels.

China and the HBM export ban

In December 2024 the United States restricted exports of HBM, the tools to make it and advanced packaging equipment to China, and added more than 140 Chinese chip firms to its Entity List. Because HBM is the memory every frontier AI chip needs, the rules target the bottleneck rather than the chip.

  • CXMT, China's leading DRAM maker, targets HBM3 mass production by the end of 2026, with early yields reported around 25% for 8-high stacks; small-scale HBM3E production was reported in August 2026 but not confirmed by the company. Estimates put it one to two generations, or three to four years, behind.
  • Huawei has relied mainly on HBM stockpiled from Samsung (and to a lesser extent SK hynix) and announced its own "proprietary" HBM in September 2025.
  • One estimate projects about 7 million mostly HBM3 dies from China in 2026; its author calls the figure highly uncertain.

Ways over the wall

There are two broad strategies: build a wider pipe, or send fewer bytes through it. Pick an approach.

What to watch to 2028

📈 Supply

Whether HBM stays sold out into 2027, how fast SK hynix spends its listing proceeds, Samsung's share of Rubin, and when consumer DRAM prices fall.

🧪 Technology

HBM4E and custom base dies in 2027, high-bandwidth flash samples and first products, CXL pools in production inference, and whether SRAM inference chips win share after Nvidia's Groq deal.

🌏 Geopolitics

CXMT's HBM3 yields and any HBM3E confirmation, tighter or looser export rules, and Huawei's stockpile running down.

🧭 Closing

🎯 The bottom line AI's limiting resource inside the chip is not maths; it is moving data. Because generating each token means re-reading the whole model, memory bandwidth sets the speed limit, memory capacity sets how many users and how much context fit, and memory now makes up most of an accelerator's component cost. That is why three memory makers have become as strategic as Nvidia, why export controls target HBM, and why your next laptop costs more. The way over the wall is both a wider pipe (HBM4, custom base dies, high-bandwidth flash, SRAM chips) and fewer bytes (batching, quantization, smarter KV caches). Watch the memory roadmap as closely as the GPU roadmap.
